tldr: To tackle foothold-constrained terrain like stepping stones and gaps, the authors propose "WM-LOCO," a framework that jointly trains a recurrent world model (RSSM) and reinforcement learning (PPO) end-to-end to predict near-future observations and walk with anticipatory lookahead—without explicit foothold planning. In simulation, it achieved high success rates on gaps and stepping stones where standard methods completely failed. On a physical Unitree G1 humanoid, it reached an average success rate of 93.3% fully onboard using only a single depth stream.
overview:
When humans cross stepping stones or jump across gaps, we do not just stare at our feet. We look several steps ahead, anticipate where to place each foot, and prepare in advance. However, conventional reinforcement learning for bipedal robots assumes continuous, flat ground with footholds everywhere, relying heavily on immediate visual information for control. On foothold-constrained terrain—such as stepping stones, narrow stair treads, or gaps—a single misstep instantly leads to a fall.

Prior approaches have used complex pipelines: explicitly specifying foothold locations, multi-stage distillation from privileged experts, or computing foot placements using online mathematical optimization. The authors asked: "Could a learned world model that summarizes and predicts near-future observations and rewards naturally enable anticipatory walking, without explicit foothold labels or staged learning?"

The proposed method, "WM-LOCO," combines a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), training them jointly end-to-end. In simulation evaluations, WM-LOCO cleared gaps and stepping stones with over 78% success, where a baseline PPO failed completely with a 0% success rate. On stairs, it increased stride length and significantly reduced pelvis acceleration. Furthermore, deployed on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid using only an onboard single depth camera and proprioception (joint angles, IMU, etc.), it achieved an outstanding average success rate of 93.3% across challenging real-world terrains.
contributions: Proposed WM-LOCO, a simple visual locomotion framework that jointly trains a recurrent world model (RSSM) and PPO without explicit foothold labels or multi-stage distillation on challenging foothold-constrained terrain
Achieved high traversal success rates of 78.2% to 100% in simulation on gap and stepping stone tasks where a baseline PPO achieved a 0% success rate

Significantly improved locomotion quality on stairs while matching baseline success rates, extending stride length (+15% to +35%), suppressing pelvis acceleration (-24% to -33%), and reducing normalized mechanical energy consumption (6% to 20%)

Demonstrated fully onboard deployment on a physical Unitree G1 humanoid using only a single depth stream and proprioception on a Jetson Orin, achieving an average success rate of 93.3% across three terrain classes

sections.heading: Why Do Bipedal Robots Need Anticipatory Lookahead?
sections.summary: On foothold-constrained terrain like stepping stones and gaps, a single misstep causes an immediate fall, making the ability to anticipate several steps ahead essential—just like in humans. Prior methods relied on complex multi-stage pipelines or explicit planning, but this work provides a simpler solution by jointly training a world model.
sections.details:
When humans and bipedal animals navigate stairs, gaps, or stepping stones, they subconsciously look several steps ahead to predict viable foot placements and prepare the next step before their foot even touches down. In contrast, existing deep reinforcement learning locomotion policies are often trained on continuous terrain where foot contacts are viable anywhere, deciding actions based solely on immediate observations or brief temporal histories.

While this works on flat ground, it proves fatal on foothold-constrained terrain where feasible foot contacts are sparse, discontinuous, or geometrically restricted, such as stepping stones, gaps, or narrow stair treads. Unlike quadrupeds, a bipedal robot that misses a foothold is left with only a single support leg to recover, so a single mistake leads directly to a fall.

To tackle this challenge, prior studies introduced complex mechanisms: multi-stage reward design, distillation from privileged teachers, or online foothold planners based on mixed-integer quadratic programming. However, these lead to heavy implementation and training pipelines. Although world models have been applied to locomotion, they were mostly evaluated on stairs and rough terrain, leaving unanswered the fundamental question of how effective predictive signals are in environments where footholds are extremely sparse.

This paper proposes WM-LOCO (World-Model-Augmented Visual Locomotion), which jointly trains a recurrent world model and PPO end-to-end. Without complex distillation, external planners, or foothold labels, simply feeding the predictive recurrent features generated by the world model to the policy allows the humanoid robot to traverse difficult foothold-constrained terrain with ease.

sections.heading: Architecture: Jointly Training the World Model and Locomotion Policy
sections.summary: WM-LOCO builds a recurrent world model (RSSM) that predicts near-future observations and rewards from proprioception and a single depth image, feeding its internal memory to the PPO policy. To address sparse reward issues on foothold-constrained terrain, it introduces geometric foot-contact reward shaping for stairs and stepping stones.
sections.details:
The core framework relies on a cooperative synergy between the world model, which anticipates near-future environmental changes, and the PPO policy, which receives those predictions to select actions.

### 2.1 Forward-Aware World-Model Policy
The locomotion task is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). At each timestep $t$, the policy receives a 5-frame proprioceptive history $p_{t}$ (joint positions, velocities, IMU, and previous actions), a single depth image $d_{t}$ from the head camera, and a target velocity command $c_{t}$.

The world model uses a Recurrent State Space Model (RSSM) consisting of a deterministic hidden state $h_{t}$ and a stochastic latent variable $z_{t}$ (128-dimensional). It comprises a transition model that updates memory from prior state and action, a posterior that infers latents from current observations, a prior that predicts latents from memory alone without observations, and decoders that reconstruct depth, proprioception, and rewards. The training loss $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WM}}$ is the sum of reconstruction errors and KL divergence.

A key design decision is that, instead of offline pretraining or replay buffers, the PPO surrogate loss and $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{WM}}$ are jointly optimized in a single objective via gradient updates. Only a predictive feature $f^{\mathrm{WM}}_{t}$, linearly projected from the world model's deterministic memory $h_{t}$, is passed to the policy. At inference time, there is no need to roll out (imagine) future trajectories; it operates lightweight as a standard recurrent network.

### 2.2 Training Reward
On foothold-constrained terrain, the delay from an initial misstep to a fall is significant, making standard velocity-tracking rewards far too sparse to signal success or failure. Using a foot volume-point set sampled on the foot mesh, the authors introduce the following geometric reward shaping:

- **Stair Border Penalty**: Penalizes stepping on the flat floor beside the stairs, preventing the robot from bypassing obstacles to cheat velocity rewards.
- **Riser Intrusion Penalty**: Penalizes the toes hitting the vertical face (riser) of a stair. Excluding the top 4 cm avoids false triggers during diagonal landings on tread edges, preventing frequent tripping on hardware.
- **Sequential Stair Tread Contact Reward**: Indexes tread regions as $R_1, R_2, \dots$ along the heading direction and rewards alternating left-right foot contacts within a time window matching the forward velocity.
- **Stepping Stone Top Contact Reward**: Does not enforce stepping order; instead, it rewards landing on the valid top surface of a stone within the current tile, shaping the robot to target the stone's center.

sections.heading: Evaluation Design: Rigorous Simulation and Unitree G1 Hardware
sections.summary: The Unitree G1 was trained across 8,192 parallel environments in IsaacLab and compared against a baseline PPO across three terrain classes (gaps, stepping stones, stairs) with three difficulty tiers each. Perturbations and domain randomization were deliberately omitted to rigorously isolate foothold adaptation and gait quality.
sections.details:
To verify the effectiveness of the proposed method, rigorous comparative experiments were conducted in both simulation and the real world.

### Setup
IsaacLab was used as the simulator, running 8,192 environments in parallel on a single NVIDIA RTX 5880-Ada (48 GB). The robot is the Unitree G1 humanoid. Emulating an Intel RealSense D435 head camera, depth images rendered at $64\times 36$ are cropped to $32\times 18$, clipped to a range of $0.1\text{--}2.5\,\mathrm{m}$, and captured at 50 Hz. Stairs, gaps, and stepping stones are procedurally generated, with parameters varying by difficulty level (Easy, Medium, Hard).

### Baseline and Evaluation Protocol
The baseline is a standard PPO model with only the world model path and auxiliary losses removed. The shared encoder, AMP (Adversarial Motion Priors for natural locomotion posture), MoE (Mixture of Experts) backbone, reward formulation, and training iteration count are strictly identical. Consequently, any performance gap stems purely from the presence or absence of the world model's predictive features.

Evaluations used unseen terrain instances, defining "success" as the robot's center of mass crossing the goal line within 45 seconds. On stairs, in addition to success rate, gait quality metrics were measured: stride length, step count per meter, normalized mechanical energy consumption, and pelvis acceleration.

sections.heading: Baseline Hits 0% on Gaps and Stones; WM-LOCO Delivers Dominant Traversal and Smooth Gait
sections.summary: In simulation, the baseline achieved a 0.0% success rate across all difficulties on gaps and stepping stones, whereas WM-LOCO recorded 78.2% to 100%. On stairs, WM-LOCO matched or exceeded baseline success rates while substantially improving gait efficiency, and achieved 93.3% success on the physical Unitree G1.
sections.details:
The experimental results revealed a stark contrast.

### Success Rate Comparison (Simulation)
On Gaps and Stepping Stones, the baseline PPO scored a **0.0% success rate** across all difficulty levels from Easy to Hard. When a misstep causes an immediate fall, instantaneous observations provide insufficient lead time to adjust stride length. In contrast, WM-LOCO maintained remarkably high success rates: 90.0% to 100% on gaps, and 78.2% to 88.3% on stepping stones.

On Stairs, where foothold constraints are comparatively milder, the baseline held up with 87.0% to 91.4%, but WM-LOCO still surpassed it with 92.0% to 95.7%.

### Analysis of Failure Modes
On stepping stones, 61.0% of baseline failures were falls and 36.0% were getting stuck, with most breaking down within the first few steps from the start. For WM-LOCO, failures were rarely falls (only 1.9%); instead, 23.0% were constraint violations where a foot landed slightly outside the stone boundary. Rather than collapsing due to loss of balance, the robot simply missed the target footprint slightly, demonstrating superior control stability.

### Locomotion Quality on Stairs
While the difference in success rate on stairs was only a few percentage points, the difference in locomotion quality was pronounced. Compared to the baseline, WM-LOCO increased stride length by 15% to 35% and decreased steps per meter by 9% to 21%. Furthermore, pelvis acceleration was reduced by 24% to 33%, and normalized mechanical energy consumption dropped by 6% to 20%. Because the world model anticipates upcoming steps, the robot strides smoothly and efficiently rather than taking hesitant, shuffling steps.

### World Model Reconstruction Accuracy
Examining the world model decoder's mean squared error (MSE), depth reconstruction dropped below $1\times 10^{-3}$ after a one-step warmup, and proprioception remained below $5\times 10^{-4}$. This confirms that the world model accurately captures multimodal observations within its internal representation.

### Sim-to-Real Hardware Validation
The trained policy was exported to ONNX and run fully onboard on the Unitree G1's internal Jetson Orin. No external cameras, prior maps, or specialized state estimators were used. Across stepping stones (0.25 m width, 0.45 m spacing), stairs (0.15 m riser, 0.25 m tread), and a 0.8 m gap cleared in a single step, the robot achieved an average success rate of 93.3% across 10 trials each, reproducing contact patterns strikingly similar to simulation.

sections.heading: Current Limitations and Future Horizons
sections.summary: This method targets discrete footholds and narrow treads; extending it to continuous narrow paths like balance beams, stones with height variations, or unstructured outdoor terrain will require new reward shaping. Furthermore, testing remains limited to a single robot and the RSSM architecture.
sections.details:
Despite impressive results, the authors candidly note several limitations of WM-LOCO:

- **Terrain Scope**: The focus was on clearly foothold-constrained terrain like discrete pads and fixed-dimension stairs. Terrain where lateral and vertical constraints interact complexly—such as continuous lateral constraints on a narrow beam or stones with randomized elevations—may not be sufficiently handled by current reward shaping alone. Unstructured outdoor environments like rubble or steep slopes are also out of scope.
- **Single Morphology and Architecture**: Experiments were conducted exclusively on a single bipedal platform (Unitree G1) and a single world model architecture (RSSM). However, because the policy receives an abstracted recurrent feature, swapping in other architectures, such as Transformer-based world models, should be straightforward. Generalizing across other robot morphologies remains future work.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Anticipation Unlocks New Traversal Capabilities for Humanoids
sections.summary: By training PPO and a world model cooperatively end-to-end, WM-LOCO dramatically enhances humanoid locomotion on foothold-constrained terrain. It offers a simple, powerful approach that operates in the real world using only a single depth stream and onboard compute.
sections.details:
This study clearly demonstrates the power of anticipatory representations from recurrent world models for bipedal control in severely constrained environments.

Without supervised foothold annotations or multi-stage distillation pipelines, simply optimizing a world model jointly with reinforcement learning allows the robot to acquire internal representations predicting future observations and rewards. This enables it to conquer challenging terrain where baselines slip and fall. The 93.3% success rate on the physical Unitree G1 is especially impactful given its lightweight deployment—relying only on a single depth camera and an onboard edge computer (Jetson Orin). It marks a major milestone toward integrating vision and predictive motor control for robots navigating unknown, difficult terrain.

sections.heading: Appendix: Procedural Terrain Parameters and Locomotion Metrics
sections.summary: The appendix details terrain dimensions used in simulation and hardware, reward weight configurations, world model reconstruction errors, and breakdown data for locomotion metrics (stride length, energy consumption, pelvis acceleration) across difficulty tiers on stairs.
sections.details:
The appendix provides detailed data valuable for reproduction and analysis.

### Terrain Parameters (Appendix A)
Difficulties were chosen from a 10-level grid, selecting row 1 (Easy), row 4 (Medium), and row 9 (Hard). For example, gap widths increased across difficulties, testing up to a wide 0.8 m gap on hardware—demanding a substantial stride for a humanoid. Stepping stones had a top surface width of 0.25 m and longitudinal spacing of 0.45 m, requiring high placement precision.

### Detailed Locomotion Metrics (Appendix E)
Locomotion quality data on stairs (Table 4) shows WM-LOCO consistently outperforming the baseline across all difficulty levels. Beyond increased stride length (up to +35%) and fewer steps (up to -21%), vertical pelvis acceleration was significantly reduced, which likely contributes indirectly to stabilizing the head camera's view. Moreover, actuator torque headroom and action rate of change remained lower, confirming a smooth, hardware-friendly control behavior.

takeaways: On foothold-constrained terrain (stepping stones, gaps), standard RL relying on instantaneous vision fails completely (0% success), making anticipatory representations that predict ahead essential
Jointly training PPO and a recurrent world model (RSSM) produces powerful predictive features without requiring complex multi-stage distillation or external planners
World models not only enable successful traversal of difficult terrain, but also elevate overall gait quality by increasing stride length, lowering pelvis acceleration, and saving energy
The policy runs fully onboard in real time (50 Hz) on an edge computer (Jetson Orin) using only a single depth stream and proprioception
limitations: Terrain with coupled lateral and vertical constraints—such as stepping stones with varying elevations or narrow balance beams—requires specialized reward tuning
Empirical validation is limited to a single compact humanoid (Unitree G1) and the RSSM architecture; larger humanoids and alternative world model backbones remain untested
Unstructured outdoor environments like mud and rubble, as well as dynamically moving obstacles, are not currently addressed
